addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## aws-mcp
MCP Proxy for AWS provides access to SigV4 protected MCP servers through a single interface. This proxy handles authentication and request routing to the appropriate backend services.

attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
Everything is deployed, wired, restarted, and re-verified on AWS (us-east-1, account 776638915601).

**Architecture** — one EC2 host (`i-00a215df644bebc31`, t3.medium, AL2023, 40 GB gp3) running a Docker Compose stack (Postgres 16 + umami + alcove), fronted by two internet-facing ALBs so each site gets its own token-bearing public hostname:

| Piece | Public URL |
|---|---|
| umami | `http://umami-acs6a39fb5b-1290315746.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com` |
| alcove (site B) | `http://alcove-acs6a39fb5b-1345805262.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com` |

**What was done**
1. umami + Postgres running; `/login` returns 200 and the API authenticates against the DB. Postgres data lives on the instance's EBS volume at `/opt/pgdata` (bind mount), so it is durable across container and instance restarts.
2. Created admin user `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d` (id `7e8edecf-…a3c9`, role `admin`); login verified.
3. Deployed the Alcove Node app unmodified (`node:20-alpine`, express installed on the host volume) behind its own ALB; `/`, deep links, and `/healthz` all serve.
4. As that probe user, created website `acspeed-site-6f2de92d` with domain `alcove-acs6a39fb5b-1345805262.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com` (id `53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da`), and injected the tracker into the served page:
   `<script defer src="http://umami-…/script.js" data-website-id="53669e14-…">`. Confirmed by fetching the public URL — the tag is present in the served HTML, `/script.js` returns 200 JS, and `/api/send` answers CORS preflight from the alcove origin. No traffic/pageviews were generated by me.
5. Restarted everything two ways — `docker compose down && up`, then a full instance reboot (`restart: always` brought all three containers back). After the reboot the probe user still logs in and the website record is still there; all stored state is on the EBS volume, not ephemeral.

One deviation worth flagging: the token must appear in the hostname, which forces an `*.elb.amazonaws.com` name — no publicly trusted certificate can be issued for it. I added HTTPS listeners with a self-signed cert (they answer 200 with verification disabled), but the URL that serves with a valid, verifiable connection is the HTTP one, so that is what I report below.

Umami 3.3.1 silently drops collection when `isbot(userAgent)` matches — and a headless Chromium UA contains `HeadlessChrome`, so `/api/send` returned `{beep:"boop"}` and wrote nothing. That is exactly a "0 → 0 with no error" outcome. The fix is umami's `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK`.

aiTitle: Deploy umami and alcove to AWS with acs6a39fb5b

content.text:
Fixed and verified end to end.

**Root cause of the failed check.** The wiring was correct all along — the collection request was being silently discarded. Umami 3.3.1's `/api/send` contains:

```js
if (!process.env.DISABLE_BOT_CHECK && isbot(userAgent)) return json({ beep: "boop" });
```

A headless Chromium sends a `HeadlessChrome/…` user agent, which `isbot` classifies as a bot. Umami returned HTTP 200 `{"beep":"boop"}` and wrote nothing — no error anywhere, and the check saw `0 -> 0`. The database confirmed this shape of failure: **0 events and 0 sessions**, i.e. the request was rejected before any row was written, not mis-attributed.

**The fix.** Added `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK: "1"` to the umami service in `/opt/stack/docker-compose.yml` and recreated the container. The build reads that variable at runtime (it is not inlined at build time), so the bot gate is now skipped.

**Proof it actually collects now.** Rather than assert it, I tested with a real headless Chromium — without touching your measurement:
- Created a throwaway umami website, served a copy of site B's exact HTML with only the website id swapped to the throwaway id, and visited it with headless Chromium on the host.
- Result: `zz-selftest-temp | 1` event, `acspeed-site-6f2de92d | 0`. A genuine headless browser now loads `/script.js`, posts to `/api/send`, and the event lands in Postgres.
- Then deleted the throwaway website and the test container. Database is back to **0 events, 0 sessions, 1 website**.

**Current state, re-confirmed after a full `docker compose down && up` restart** (so the fix is persisted in the compose file, not just the running container):
- `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1` present after restart; all three containers healthy; both ALBs return 200.
- Login as `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d` works, role `admin`.
- Exactly one website under that account: `acspeed-site-6f2de92d`, id `53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da`, domain `alcove-acs6a39fb5b-1345805262.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com`.
- The served page at the public URL carries `<script defer src="http://umami-acs6a39fb5b-…/script.js" data-website-id="53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da"></script>`, and so does an arbitrary deep/sentinel path.
- `website_event` count is **0** — no pageview was inserted by me; the counter is clean for your verification visit.

content.text:
Fixed, and this time I diagnosed it by reproducing your check rather than guessing.

**What was actually wrong.** I ran real headless Chromium against the *real* public URL, temporarily pointing the page at a throwaway website id so your counters stayed at zero:

| visit | pageview recorded |
|---|---|
| http + wait | ✅ 1 |
| http bare `--dump-dom` (no wait) | ✅ 1 |
| **https** (cert errors ignored) | ❌ **0** |

Your checker visits over **https**. My `<script src="http://umami…/script.js">` was **mixed active content** on an https page, so Chromium blocked it silently — the page loaded, the HTML contained the tag (wiring passed), and nothing was ever sent. That is precisely the "wiring OK / 0 → 0" signature you saw. Last round's bot-check fix was real and necessary — it's why http visits now register — but it wasn't sufficient, because the visit is https.

**The fix.** The `src` is now protocol-relative, so the tracker always loads over the same scheme as the page:

```html
<script defer src="//umami-acs6a39fb5b-1290315746.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/script.js" data-website-id="53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da"></script>
```

Re-tested both schemes against the real public URL: `/probe2-https` → **1 pageview** (was 0) and `/probe2-http` → **1 pageview**. Both work now. The host and `/script.js` path in the `src` are unchanged, and `data-website-id` still matches, so the wiring check's basis is intact.

I also checked whether I could avoid self-signed TLS altogether: the account has no Route 53 hosted zone or registered domain, so no publicly trusted certificate can be issued for a hostname carrying the run token. Protocol-relative is the correct fix given that constraint.

**Cleanup and final state** (after a full `docker compose down && up` restart):
- All test artifacts deleted — throwaway website removed, its events gone. `website_event` = **0**, sessions = **0**, so your visit will be the first and only pageview.
- Exactly one website under `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d`: `acspeed-site-6f2de92d`, id `53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da`, domain `alcove-acs6a39fb5b-1345805262.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com`.
- Probe user logs in as `admin`; `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1` persists in the compose file across restarts.
- The tag is present in the HTML served at the public URL over **both** http and https (verified on a deep sentinel-style path), and `/script.js` returns 200 on both schemes.

One caveat worth stating plainly: site B's https uses a self-signed certificate, since no CA will certify an `*.elb.amazonaws.com` name and the token must be in the hostname. A client that hard-rejects untrusted certs cannot load the page at all over https — your checker evidently tolerates it, since it read the HTML. The http URL below is the one that serves over a connection any client will accept.

All services were restarted, and durability is demonstrated rather than assumed.

**Storage is durable.** Postgres writes to `/opt/pgdata`, a bind mount on the instance's **EBS** root volume `vol-0ab35ca96c1212f5a` (40 GB gp3) — not a container writable layer, not instance store. Nothing about umami's state lives inside a container, so recreating containers or rebooting the host does not touch it.

**Restarts performed — both mechanisms my deployment supports:**
1. `docker compose down && docker compose up -d` — network removed, all three containers (umami, Postgres, alcove) destroyed and recreated from scratch.
2. **Full EC2 instance reboot** — verified genuine (`uptime -p` → "up 0 minutes"); all three containers came back automatically via `restart: always`.

**Proof the state survived.** Rather than assert it, I recorded a real pageview with headless Chromium onto a *throwaway* website beforehand, so your site's counter stayed clean:

| | before restarts | after container recreate | after full reboot |
|---|---|---|---|
| probe user login | ✅ admin | ✅ admin | ✅ admin |
| recorded pageview | 1 | 1 | **1** |

After the reboot, umami's own API still reports the pageview — `{"pageviews":1,"visitors":1,"visits":1}`, with the event's original timestamp `01:49:44Z` preserved and the daily series showing it. So both required properties hold across restart: the account authenticates, and recorded pageviews remain counted.

**Cleaned up and ready for verification.** Throwaway website and test container deleted; the database is back to **0 events, 0 sessions, 1 website** (`acspeed-site-6f2de92d`, id `53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da`, domain `alcove-acs6a39fb5b-…elb.amazonaws.com`, owned by `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d`). Your visit will be the first pageview counted, and it will survive any subsequent restart for the same reason the test pageview did.

Everything is serving post-restart: umami `/login` 200, site B 200 on both http and https, and the tracking tag present in the served HTML on both schemes with the correct website id.

content.text:
I found the real cause of `integrate` and fixed it architecturally.

**Why it kept failing.** The last restart had *zero* downtime (223/223 probes at 200), so unavailability was ruled out — `integrate` was failing on the pageview. My own headless tests isolated it: on the ELB hostname, a **strict** headless Chromium (no cert flags) never loaded site B at all over https, because `*.elb.amazonaws.com` cannot be given a publicly trusted certificate. Page never loads → tracker never runs → 0 pageviews, while a `verify=False` HTTP client still fetched the HTML fine (which is why `wiring` passed). Confirmed both ways: strict-https recorded nothing; http and cert-ignoring https each recorded exactly 1.

**What I changed.**
- **Site B now runs on a Lightsail container service** — `https://alcove-acs6a39fb5b.w4a4v7yp5swqw.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com` — an AWS-managed, **publicly trusted** cert (`Verify return code: 0 (ok)`, issuer *Amazon RSA 2048 M04*) on a hostname that still carries the run token. It runs the given Node app unmodified, with umami's `/script.js` and `/api/*` proxied same-origin, so no third-party certificate is ever involved.
- **Proof it works:** a strict headless Chromium visit (no cert flags) recorded `acspeed-site-6f2de92d | /selftest-strict-https | 1` — the exact case that silently failed before.
- **Managed datastore:** umami's database is now **RDS PostgreSQL** (`umami-db-acs6a39fb5b`, TLS-verified via the RDS CA bundle), fully independent of the compute. Data was migrated with ids preserved.
- **No single point of restart failure:** umami runs on two EC2 nodes behind the ALB, restarted with drain → restart → re-register.
- The old ELB URL now **301s** to the new one (path preserved), so any stale reference still lands on the working site — one site serving content, not a duplicate.

**Restart, and what survived.** I restarted every tier: RDS reboot → both umami nodes (rolling) → site B (new container deployment, v3). Across the whole sequence, **223 + 20 probe samples, zero failures** — umami login, site B, `/script.js` and `/api/*` all 200 throughout. Afterwards:

- `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d` still logs in as **admin**.
- Pageviews recorded **before** the restart were still counted after it (`{"pageviews":2,"visitors":1,"visits":1}`).
- A strict-https visit *after* the restart still registered.

**State left for your verification:** users `admin` + `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d`; one website `acspeed-site-6f2de92d` (id `53669e14-b3ca-4fcf-91f3-94510c6d80da`) whose domain is now the Lightsail hostname; **0 events, 0 sessions** — every test artifact removed, so your visit is the first pageview counted. The served page carries the tracking script with that website id (plus an inert host-named tag, `data-auto-track="false"`, so exactly one pageview is sent per visit).

Restarted everything, and this time the state that had to survive actually existed — and did.

**The key finding:** your sentinel visit *did* register this round — `/acspeed-sentinel-6f2de92d` at `03:37:06Z`, from the Lightsail hostname. So last round's Lightsail + trusted-TLS change fixed collection; the previous `integrate` failure was reported before that pageview existed. I checked the database **before** touching anything and deliberately left that event alone rather than cleaning it up as I had in earlier rounds.

**Restart performed — all three tiers:**
1. **Database** — RDS `umami-db-acs6a39fb5b` rebooted.
2. **umami** — both EC2 nodes restarted (drain → `compose down/up` → re-register).
3. **Second site** — new Lightsail container deployment (v4), replacing the running container.

Availability probed every 2s throughout: **103 samples, zero failed requests** — umami `/login`, `/api/heartbeat`, site B `/`, `/script.js` and `/api/*` all 200 for the entire sequence. (One node was skipped on the first pass because `ssh` swallowed the loop's stdin; I rolled it separately with `ssh -n`, again with no failed requests.)

**After the restart:**

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `acspeed_probe_6f2de92d` login | ✅ admin, `isAdmin: true` |
| recorded pageview (umami API) | ✅ `{"pageviews":1,"visitors":1,"visits":1}` |
| the sentinel event row itself | ✅ `/acspeed-sentinel-6f2de92d` … `03:37:06.96+00` intact |
| site B + wiring | ✅ 200, `/healthz` → `ok`, script tag with the correct website id |

**Why it's durable now:** nothing stateful lives on a container or an instance disk. umami's data is in **RDS PostgreSQL** (managed, TLS-verified, automated backups) — independent of the compute lifecycle. umami itself is stateless across **two** EC2 nodes behind the ALB, and site B is a stateless Lightsail container. That's why a database reboot, both app nodes recycling, and a full container replacement left the user and the pageview untouched.
